title: The hare “cheweth the cud” — the Greek of the same verse says “does not”
summary: The KJV, with the Hebrew, says of both the coney and the hare that each “cheweth the cud”. In Brenton’s Greek the second of the two animals is unclean “because it does not chew the cud”.
text: KJV Leviticus 11:5: “And the coney, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you.” KJV 11:6: “And the hare, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you.” Hebrew (WLC) 11:5: וְאֶת־הַשָּׁפָ֗ן כִּֽי־מַעֲלֵ֤ה גֵרָה֙ ה֔וּא [and the shaphan, because it brings up the cud]. 11:6: וְאֶת־הָאַרְנֶ֗בֶת כִּֽי־מַעֲלַ֤ת גֵּרָה֙ הִ֔וא [and the arnebeth, because it brings up the cud]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 11:5: Καὶ τὸν δασύποδα, ὅτι ἀνάγει μηρυκισμὸν τοῦτο, καὶ ὁπλὴν οὐ διχηλεῖ [and the dasypous, because this brings up the cud and does not divide the hoof]. 11:6: Καὶ τὸν χοιρογρύλλιον, ὅτι οὐκ ἀνάγει μηρυκισμὸν τοῦτο, καὶ ὁπλὴν οὐ διχηλεῖ [and the choirogryllios, because this does not bring up the cud and does not divide the hoof]. KJV Deuteronomy 14:7: “as the camel, and the hare, and the coney: for they chew the cud, but divide not the hoof” Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Deuteronomy 14:7: τὸν κάμηλον, καὶ δασύποδα, καὶ χοιρογρύλλιον· ὅτι ἀνάγουσι μηρυκισμὸν, καὶ ὁπλὴν οὐ διχηλοῦσιν [the camel and dasypous and choirogryllios, because they bring up the cud and do not divide the hoof]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/3/11/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/LEV11.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/DEU14.htm.
reasoning: In the KJV and the Hebrew quoted, verses 5 and 6 give the same reason for each animal: it chews the cud but does not divide the hoof. Brenton’s Greek gives that reason in verse 5, but in verse 6 it has a negative, “does not bring up the cud”. So in the Greek of verse 6 the animal fails both tests, where in the KJV it passes one.
scope: G applies at Leviticus 11:6 only. This compares two published wordings of one verse. Brenton’s Greek of Deuteronomy 14:7 says that both animals do chew the cud, so the Greek edition is not consistent with itself on this point; this record does not say which wording is original. The animal names are left untranslated in the brackets because their identification is not settled here. No claim is made about whether any animal in fact chews the cud. title: “Her purification” or “their purification”? The law names only the mother

title: Every ox, lamb or goat killed — or only those killed as offerings? The Greek is longer
summary: In the KJV, with the Hebrew, anyone of the house of Israel who kills an ox, lamb or goat and does not bring it to the tabernacle is guilty of blood. Brenton’s Greek adds the strangers to those bound by the rule, and adds a clause naming the purpose: to make it a burnt offering or a peace offering.
text: KJV Leviticus 17:3: “What man soever there be of the house of Israel, that killeth an ox, or lamb, or goat, in the camp, or that killeth it out of the camp,” KJV 17:4: “And bringeth it not unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, to offer an offering unto the Lord before the tabernacle of the Lord; blood shall be imputed unto that man” Hebrew (WLC) 17:3: אִ֥ישׁ אִישׁ֙ מִבֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל [any man of the house of Israel]. 17:4: וְאֶל־פֶּ֜תַח אֹ֣הֶל מֹועֵד֮ לֹ֣א הֱבִיאֹו֒ לְהַקְרִ֤יב קָרְבָּן֙ לַֽיהוָ֔ה [and has not brought it to the door of the tent of meeting, to offer an offering to the LORD]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 17:3: ἄνθρωπος ἄνθρωπος τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ, ἢ τῶν προσηλύτων τῶν προσκειμένων ἐν ὑμῖν [any man of the sons of Israel, or of the strangers attached among you]. 17:4: καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν θύραν τῆς σκηνῆς τοῦ μαρτυρίου μὴ ἐνέγκῃ, ὥστε ποιῆσαι αὐτὸ εἰς ὁλοκαύτωμα ἢ σωτήριον Κυρίῳ δεκτὸν εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας· καὶ ὃς ἂν σφάξῃ ἔξω, καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν θύραν τῆς σκηνῆς τοῦ μαρτυρίου μὴ ἐνέγκῃ αὐτὸ, ὥστε προσενέγκαι δῶρον τῷ Κυρίῳ ἀπέναντι τῆς σκηνῆς Κυρίου [and does not bring it to the door of the tent of witness, so as to make it a whole burnt offering or a peace offering to the Lord, acceptable for a sweet smell; and whoever kills it outside, and does not bring it to the door of the tent of witness, so as to offer a gift to the Lord before the tent of the Lord]. reasoning: Two things stand in the Greek and not in the KJV or the Hebrew quoted. In 17:3 the Greek extends the rule to strangers; the KJV of 17:3 names only the house of Israel. In 17:4 the Greek has a whole extra clause that speaks of making the animal “a whole burnt offering or a peace offering”, before it repeats the clause the KJV has. The KJV of 17:3–4 speaks of any killing of these animals, in the camp or out of it.

The KJV names strangers later in the chapter, but not in this rule. title: The sheaf waved “on the morrow after the sabbath” — the Greek says “on the morrow of the first”
summary: The KJV, with the Hebrew, has the priest wave the sheaf “on the morrow after the sabbath”. Brenton’s Greek has no sabbath in the verse: the sheaf is lifted “on the morrow of the first”, which points back to the first day of unleavened bread.
text: KJV Leviticus 23:7: “In the first day ye shall have an holy convocation” KJV 23:11: “And he shall wave the sheaf before the Lord, to be accepted for you: on the morrow after the sabbath the priest shall wave it.” KJV 23:15: “And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the sabbath” Hebrew (WLC) 23:11: מִֽמָּחֳרַת֙ הַשַּׁבָּ֔ת יְנִיפֶ֖נּוּ הַכֹּהֵֽן [on the morrow of the sabbath the priest shall wave it]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 23:7: Καὶ ἡμέρα ἡ πρώτη κλητὴ ἁγία ἔσται ὑμῖν [and the first day shall be a holy convocation for you]. 23:11: τῇ ἐπαύριον τῆς πρώτης ἀνοίσει αὐτό ὁ ἱερεύς [on the morrow of the first the priest shall lift it up]. 23:15: ἀπὸ τῆς ἐπαύριον τῶν σαββάτων [from the morrow of the sabbaths]. 23:16: ἕως τῆς ἐπαύριον τῆς ἐσχάτης ἑβδομάδος [until the morrow of the last week]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/3/23/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/LEV23.htm.
reasoning: The KJV dates the waving of the sheaf from “the sabbath” and does not say which sabbath. Brenton’s Greek at 23:11 dates it from “the first”, a feminine form that matches “the first day” of 23:7. On the Greek wording the sheaf is waved on a fixed day of the month, the day after the first day of the feast. On the KJV wording the day depends on which sabbath is meant. The count of fifty days in 23:15–16 starts from the same day, so the difference carries over to the date of the feast that follows.
scope: G applies at Leviticus 23:11 only. At 23:15 Brenton’s Greek has “sabbaths”, as the KJV has “sabbath”; at 23:16 the Greek has “the last week” where the KJV has “the seventh sabbath”, which is not tagged here. title: Death for him that “blasphemeth the name of the Lord” — in the Greek, for him that names it
summary: In the KJV the man put to death “blasphemed the name of the Lord, and cursed”, and the law is against him that “blasphemeth the name”. Brenton’s Greek has a verb of naming: he “named the name and cursed”, and the one who “names the name of the Lord” is to die.

reasoning: The KJV’s verb, “blaspheme”, means to speak against. Brenton’s Greek uses the ordinary verbs for naming. In the story the Greek still has the man curse, but in the law of 24:16 the Greek wording makes the capital act the naming of the name, with no word of cursing or reviling in that verse. In the KJV the capital act is blasphemy.

title: The congregation sins in ignorance: a bullock as the sin offering, or a bullock burnt and a kid as the sin offering?
summary: Leviticus says that when the whole congregation sins through ignorance it offers a young bullock, and calls it “a sin offering for the congregation”. Numbers says that for a thing done in ignorance by the congregation the bullock is a burnt offering, and the sin offering is a kid of the goats.
text: KJV Leviticus 4:13: “And if the whole congregation of Israel sin through ignorance, and the thing be hid from the eyes of the assembly, and they have done somewhat against any of the commandments of the Lord concerning things which should not be done” KJV 4:14: “then the congregation shall offer a young bullock for the sin” KJV 4:21: “it is a sin offering for the congregation” KJV Numbers 15:22: “And if ye have erred, and not observed all these commandments” KJV Numbers 15:24: “if ought be committed by ignorance without the knowledge of the congregation, that all the congregation shall offer one young bullock for a burnt offering”; “and one kid of the goats for a sin offering” Hebrew (WLC) Leviticus 4:14: וְהִקְרִ֨יבוּ הַקָּהָ֜ל פַּ֤ר בֶּן־בָּקָר֙ לְחַטָּ֔את [and the assembly shall offer a young bull for a sin offering]. Numbers 15:24: וְעָשׂ֣וּ כָל־הָעֵדָ֡ה פַּ֣ר בֶּן־בָּקָר֩ אֶחָ֨ד לְעֹלָ֜ה [and all the congregation shall offer one young bull for a burnt offering]; וּשְׂעִיר־עִזִּ֥ים אֶחָ֖ד לְחַטָּֽת [and one male goat for a sin offering]. Numbers 15:24: μόσχον ἕνα ἐκ βοῶν ἄμωμον εἰς ὁλοκαύτωμα [one unblemished calf of the herd for a whole burnt offering]; καὶ χίμαρον ἐξ αἰγῶν ἕνα περὶ ἁμαρτίας [and one kid of the goats for sin]. reasoning: Both laws deal with the congregation as a whole, with an act done in ignorance and hidden from it. Leviticus requires one animal, a bullock, and it is the sin offering. title: Flying creeping things: “these may ye eat” — or “they shall not be eaten”?
summary: Leviticus forbids flying creeping things but makes an exception: four kinds, the locust among them, may be eaten. Deuteronomy says every creeping thing that flies is unclean and shall not be eaten, and names no exception among them.

title: Offerings commanded at Sinai — or “I spake not unto your fathers … concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices”?
summary: Leviticus says the law of the burnt offering and the other sacrifices is what the Lord commanded Moses in mount Sinai, in the day he commanded Israel to offer. In Jeremiah the Lord says he did not speak to the fathers or command them concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices in the day he brought them out of Egypt.
